final_answer:
Best answer: the District of South Carolina (Fourth Circuit) should indict, with moderate confidence and several caveats stated below.

1. Each office can charge only its own executions. Section 1347 punishes each knowing execution of a scheme to defraud a health care benefit program, and the maximum is 10 years per count (20 if serious bodily injury, life if death). Venue lies where an execution occurred, or under 18 U.S.C. 3237(a) where a continuing offense began, continued or was completed. The false claims were made in two states, so each district's prosecutors can charge the counts executed there. I could not fetch the text of 3237 or 1347 from a primary source (Cornell and FindLaw were blocked), so this rests on my background knowledge of those statutes.

2. The Guidelines largely erase that boundary. Under USSG 1B1.3(a)(2), fraud offenses are covered by 3D1.2(d). Conduct that is part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan counts as relevant conduct whether or not it is charged, and it need not have occurred in the sentencing district. Fraud counts group under 3D1.2(d), and loss is aggregated under 2B1.1. Whichever district prosecutes will therefore be able to sentence on the loss from both states' false claims, as long as the court finds a common scheme or same course of conduct. A search result summarizing USSC primers supports this. I did not read the primers themselves.

3. Because the total loss is likely the same in either court, the sentencing difference most likely to matter is circuit law on how much weight the commentary gets. A search result describing the split states that the Fourth Circuit still follows Stinson, giving the Guidelines commentary authoritative deference. That favors the government, because the commentary reads 'loss' as the greater of actual or intended loss. It also states that the Eleventh Circuit, under en banc United States v. Dupree, uses commentary only to interpret an ambiguous guideline. The Georgia district is in the Eleventh Circuit, so a defendant there can argue that loss is limited to actual loss. The government therefore has more room for a higher range in South Carolina. This is the central claim and it rests on secondary summaries, not the opinions. Caveat: the Sentencing Commission amended 2B1.1 effective Nov. 1, 2024 to move the actual/intended loss rule into the guideline text. I recall this but did not verify it, and if correct it shrinks the practical difference. A cert petition on commentary deference appeared in search results, and I did not research its status.

4. Other notes. Stacking is limited by 5G1.2(d): if the guideline range exceeds the statutory maximum on the highest count, sentences run consecutively to reach the total punishment. A single prosecution that charges many counts therefore lets the court run sentences consecutively up to the guideline total. Splitting the case into two prosecutions gains little. Whichever case is sentenced second faces 5G1.3, which generally adjusts for or runs concurrently the time already attributed to the same relevant conduct. I did not verify 5G1.3 text. The Southern District of Georgia remains a fully viable alternative, since the guideline range is driven by aggregate loss and enhancements such as the 2B1.1(b)(7) federal health care offense enhancement apply in either court.

Bottom line: indict in the District of South Carolina, one indictment with as many execution counts as venue allows, and ask the court to aggregate the Georgia conduct as relevant conduct. A defensible alternative view is that the choice is close to neutral, because relevant conduct pulls both states' losses into either case.
